noun: A word that names a person, place, thing or idea.
A noun names something: a person (madre), a place (ciudad), a thing (mesa) or an idea (amor). Nouns are what you can put 'the' or 'a' in front of.
verb: A word for an action or state: to eat, to be, to have.
A verb says what someone does or is: comer (to eat), ser (to be), tener (to have). Most sentences need one.
adjective: A word that describes a noun: big, red, good.
An adjective describes a noun: a big house, a good friend. In Spanish it must match the noun in gender and number: 'casa blanca', 'casas blancas', 'libro blanco'.
adverb: A word that says how, when, where or how much; it never changes form.
An adverb adds detail to a verb, an adjective or another adverb: how (bien), when (hoy), where (aquí), how much (muy). It never changes for gender or number.
preposition: A small word linking a noun to the rest of the sentence: in, to, with, for.

A preposition is a small word that links a noun to the rest of the sentence, usually showing place, time or relation: 'en la mesa' (on the table), 'a las tres' (at three), 'con mi madre' (with my mother). It always comes before its noun.
conjunction: A word that joins words or parts of a sentence: and, but, because.
A conjunction joins words or whole parts of a sentence: y (and), o (or), pero (but), porque (because), que (that), si (if).
pronoun: A word that stands in for a noun: I, you, he, it, them.
A pronoun replaces a noun so you do not repeat it: yo (I), tú (you), él (he), ella (she), nosotros (we), ellos (they). Others are objects of the action: 'lo', 'me', 'se'.
determiner: A small word before a noun saying which one or how many: the, this, my, some.
A determiner sits before a noun and pins it down: which one (este libro, that book), whose (mi libro, my book), how many (muchos libros, many books), or just 'the/a' (the **article**).
article: The tiny words for 'the' (el, la) and 'a' (un, una); they match the noun's gender.
Articles are the small words 'the' and 'a'.
number: A word for an amount or position: one, two, first.
Numbers give an amount (uno, dos, tres: cardinals) or a position (primero, segundo, tercero: ordinals).
interjection: A short exclamation that stands on its own: hello, oh, wow.
An interjection is a word that expresses a feeling or a greeting and does not link to the rest of a sentence: ¡hola! (hello), ¡ay! (ouch, oh no), ¡vaya! (wow, well), ¡ojalá! (I hope so).
gender: Every Spanish noun is masculine or feminine, and words around it match.
Every noun is either masculine or feminine, even things: 'el libro' (m), 'la mesa' (f). Gender is a label of the word, not of the thing.
plural: The 'more than one' form: add -s after a vowel, -es after a consonant.
Plural means more than one. Add -s to words ending in a vowel (casa, casas) and -es to words ending in a consonant (ciudad, ciudades). Words ending in -z change to -ces: luz, luces.
conjugation: The changing forms of a verb for who does it and when.
Conjugating a verb means giving it the ending that fits the person (I, you, he, we, they) and the time. Take hablar (to speak): hablo, hablas, habla, hablamos, hablan.
tense: The time a verb refers to: now (present), earlier (past), later (future).
Tense shows when something happens. Present: hablo (I speak). Past: hablé or hablaba (I spoke). Future: hablaré (I will speak).
participle: A verb form ending in -ado or -ido, used with 'haber' or as an adjective.
The participle is the verb form ending in -ado (for -ar verbs) or -ido (for -er and -ir verbs): hablado, comido, vivido. Irregular ones exist: hecho, dicho, visto.
gerund: The -ando / -iendo form of a verb, for an action in progress.

The gerund ends in -ando (for -ar verbs) or -iendo (for -er and -ir verbs): hablando, comiendo, viviendo. Its main use is with 'estar' to say something is happening right now: 'estoy comiendo' (I am eating).
stem-changing-verb: A verb whose vowel changes in most forms: poder becomes puedo.
In these verbs a vowel in the middle of the word changes when it carries the stress: e becomes ie (querer: quiero), o becomes ue (poder: puedo), e becomes i (pedir: pido).
irregular-verb: A verb that does not follow the usual endings; learn its forms by heart.

Most verbs follow a regular pattern for their endings. Irregular verbs break it, so their forms must be learned one by one: ser becomes soy, eres, es; ir becomes voy, vas, va; tener becomes tengo, tienes.
imperative: The verb form for commands and requests: come, speak, wait.
The imperative gives a command or instruction. For a friend (tú) the form often equals the 'he/she' form: 'habla' (speak), 'come' (eat). For a polite 'usted', use 'hable', 'coma'.
subjunctive: A verb form for wishes, doubts and things that are not (yet) fact.
The subjunctive is a set of verb forms used when the speaker is not stating plain fact: a wish, a request, a doubt, an emotion. It usually follows 'que': 'Quiero que vengas' (I want you to come).
